sections.html:
Bulloch County sits in southeast Georgia, and Statesboro is the county seat. Georgia Southern University and the East Georgia State College campus are in Statesboro, so the housing market leans toward students and the people who rent to them. The 2025 estimate is 86,949 residents, up from 81,099 in 2020. Half of occupied homes, 50.1 percent, were rented in 2020, and the median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $222,500.

A lot of sellers here hold a rental or an inherited house. Both situations bring tax questions, and the sections below cover them in the order you will probably run into them.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Bulloch County?
sections.html:
County government offices keep weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Bulloch divides the work differently than most Georgia counties: the tax assessors, not the tax commissioner, take property tax returns and homestead applications.

Bulloch County property tax offices
OfficeAddressPhoneHandles
Tax Assessors113 North Main Street, Statesboro912-764-2181Values, returns, homestead, appeals
Tax Commissioner113 North Main Street, Suite 101, Statesboro912-764-6285Billing, collection, payments

Tax questions can also go by email to propertytax@bullochcounty.net. The county has an online tax record search and a payment portal, both linked from the tax commissioner's page on the county website. Card payments carry a convenience fee that goes to the processor, not the county.

To check whether a bill is current, the online record search is quicker than a phone call. Save the phones for payoff letters, exemptions and corrections to the record.

Fair market value is set as of January 1. The tax is levied on an assessed value equal to 40 percent of that figure, and one mill is one dollar for each thousand dollars of assessed value. The county commissioners set the county rate and the school board sets its own.

Every owner files an initial return for real and personal property held on January 1. Bulloch takes returns from January 1 through April 1 at the assessors' office. That first return carries forward at the last finalized value, so you file again only after adding property, making improvements or wanting to declare a different value.

Email returns are refused. A faxed return must be in the office by 5:00 p.m. on the closing day of the filing or appeal period. The assessors cannot waive penalties or stretch a deadline, so treat each date as final.

An appeal has to be written and filed within 45 days after the date on the notice of change. Email appeals are turned away, and a fax must arrive by 5:00 p.m. on the last day.

The path has four steps:

  • File with the Board of Tax Assessors, which reviews the appeal and answers you.
  • If the board leaves the value alone, the case goes to the County Board of Equalization for a hearing.
  • When you file, you can choose arbitration in place of that hearing.
  • If you are still unhappy, you can take the matter to Superior Court.

Allowed grounds are taxability, value, and how uniform your value is against similar properties. A complaint about the size of the tax does not qualify, because the bill follows from the millage rate. The county also has a request link for property tax assessment appeals under its How Do I menu.

Each homestead exemption requires that you own the home and live in it as your legal residence on January 1. Applications run from January 1 to April 1 at the assessors' office. A granted exemption renews every year until ownership changes.

  • Standard homestead: a $2,000 deduction from the 40 percent assessed value.
  • Age 65 and up: $4,000 off state and county taxes, for households under the income cap the assessors set.
  • Age 62 and up: a school tax exemption capped at $10,000 of assessed value, with its own income cap.
  • Disabled veterans and surviving spouses of military members: larger exemptions under state law.

Homeowners 62 and older who pass an income test can also defer tax. Deferred tax generally comes due when ownership changes or the balance reaches 85 percent of the property's value, so a sale ends the deferral and the balance is paid from your proceeds.

Farm owners can apply by April 1 for a conservation use covenant. It runs ten years, costs a $10 recording fee and carries a penalty of twice the taxes saved if it is broken. Talk to the assessors before you sell covenanted land.

sections.h2: Selling a Bulloch County rental or rural tract
sections.html:
Rentals stood vacant at a 9.0 percent rate in 2020, against 1.4 percent for owner homes. Median gross rent for 2020 to 2024 is $995. A landlord selling a Statesboro rental is dealing with buyers in a county where about half of occupied homes are rented.

  • Student rentals near the university are priced and bought differently than family homes.
  • Rural tracts outside Statesboro often carry farm or timber use, so ask the assessors about covenants first.
  • The county keeps a separate timber harvest page, worth a look if trees were cut before the sale.

Pull the online tax record for the parcel before you list. It shows what the assessors have on file, so a wrong acreage or a missing exemption is easy to spot. Landlords should also check that the owner name on each bill matches the deed before closing.

sections.h2: Do Bulloch County cities send their own tax bill?
sections.html:
Four of them do. Statesboro, Brooklet, Portal and Register each bill and collect real and personal property tax on their own, so a house inside their limits draws one bill from the county and a second from the city.

That matters at closing. Your payoff request has to cover both bills, and the title company needs to know which city, if any, holds your parcel.

Get a payoff from the tax commissioner and ask whoever handles your closing how this year's share will be divided. The due date is printed on the bill itself.

sections.h2: Steps to clear taxes before a sale
sections.html:
Start by looking up the parcel on the online record search so you know whether anything is open. Next, call the tax commissioner at 912-764-6285 and ask for a written payoff that covers the county bill. If the house is inside Statesboro, Brooklet, Portal or Register, ask the city office for its own figure as well.

Give both payoff letters to the closing attorney or title company, who will pay the taxes out of your proceeds. If you hold an exemption, remember it ends with the sale and the buyer files a fresh application with the assessors by April 1. A cash buyer who skips the usual lender timeline still needs the same payoff, so ask for it early to avoid a delay on closing day.

faqs.q: Which office takes homestead applications in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessors, at 113 North Main Street in Statesboro. They accept applications from January 1 through April 1, and a granted exemption renews on its own.

faqs.q: What is the appeal window in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: It is 45 days after the notice date. File in writing, since the assessors do not take appeals by email.

faqs.q: Does a Statesboro homeowner get one tax bill or two?
faqs.a: Two. Statesboro collects its own real and personal property tax, so the county sends one bill and the city sends another every year.

faqs.q: How do I pay Bulloch County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Tax Commissioner in person at Suite 101, 113 North Main Street, Statesboro, or online through the county's payment link. Questions go to 912-764-6285, and cards add a processor fee.

faqs.q: Can the Bulloch assessors forgive a late filing penalty?
faqs.a: No. The assessors have no authority to relieve penalties or grant filing extensions, so meet each deadline.
